item.title: Rise and spread of lead-silver metallurgy deciphered from peatland archives
item.dc:creator: Hugo Delile

item.description: How mining has shaped long-term economic and political landscapes across Europe and the Mediterranean remains poorly understood, largely because archaeological evidence is spatially fragmented and ore sources are difficult to trace from atmospheric lead (Pb) records. Here, we compile Pb isotope data from environmental archives and introduce the Environmental Match Intensity Index (EMII), a metric applied to peat records to track Pb–silver (Ag) ore-supply patterns and relative changes in the integrated mining-related atmospheric Pb signal over six millennia. EMII reveals an early mining signal centered on Laurion (Greece) during the Late Neolithic/Chalcolithic, followed by Bronze Age expansion structured by maritime routes linking the Cyclades, the Troad, and Anatolian coasts. From the Iron Age onward, our results challenge the conventional Iberian-centered mining model and instead reveal a polycentric and multimodal organization rooted in west-central European districts interconnected through major fluvial corridors and complementary terrestrial and maritime routes. EMII reaches its first major peak during the Early Roman period, declines during Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages, and rises again from the High Middle Ages onward. Despite these temporal fluctuations, the overall continental distribution of the contributing mining regions remains broadly stable. By connecting environmental archives with mining, transport, and urban demand, this framework provides a scalable approach for reconstructing the long-term organization of metal production and circulation and their contribution to anthropization processes across different chrono-cultural periods and geographical settings. item.description: The mechanism driving accelerating unrest at the densely populated Campi Flegrei caldera since 2005 remains debated. Analyzing an unprecedented two-decade geochemical dataset, we show that escalating soil CO 2 fluxes closely tracks caldera uplift, revealing magmatic fluid pressurization at 3- to 4-kilometer depth and heating as the fundamental driver of the unrest. A critical magmatic gas pulse occurred between 2018 and 2022 specifically focused this outgassing beneath the Solfatara crater. Thermodynamic modeling demonstrates that an increasing mass of ascending fluid pressurizes the hydrothermal system, forcing vapor condensation within the upper kilometer. This condensation transfers latent heat to the crust. We calculate that this released thermal energy is an order of magnitude greater than that required for the 1.6-meter uplift since 2005. Ultimately, this fluid pressurization and heating drive accelerating deformation and seismicity; alongside the 2021 emergence of seismic sequences with short inter-event times, it directly signals an escalating phreatic or magmatic eruption risk. item.description: Mineral–organic interfaces regulate crystallization processes central to mineral evolution and biogeochemical cycling, yet how organic matter (OM) actively directs nucleation and growth pathways remains unresolved. Here, we reveal a pivotal role of humic acid (HA), a representative OM, in orchestrating the crystallization of Mn oxides on hematite by influencing both the spatial distribution of Mn ions and the subsequent pathways of Mn oxides nucleation and growth. Our findings reveal that mineral-associated organic matter (MAOM) facilitates the formation of fine-grained Mn oxides through a distinct three-step mechanism: i) formation of Mn-rich and Mn-poor OM domains on hematite surface, ii) catalytic oxidation of Mn(II) and nucleation of Mn ions to form primary particles within the Mn-rich domain, and iii) subsequent assembly of Mn oxide particles via particle attachment, leading to a structurally integrated Mn oxide phase (hausmannite and manganite). Spectroscopic analysis and molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that HA adopts facet-specific conformations, which modulate Mn accumulation and particle assembly. Our findings demonstrate that OM not only associates with minerals but can modify mineral–OM interfacial reactivity and crystallization pathways, offering insights into mineral crystallization mechanisms, soil evolution, and mineral–OM interactions. item.title: Mid-mantle discontinuities beneath subduction zones linked to depth-dependent deformation of bridgmanite
item.dc:creator: John Keith Magali
Sébastien Merkel

item.description: Abstract Bridgmanite, the main mineralogical phase in the Earth’s lower mantle, is intrinsically anisotropic and may therefore generate seismic anisotropy in actively-deforming regions, particularly subduction zones. The bulk of the lower mantle is widely regarded as well-mixed but recent seismic observations suggest structures at mid-mantle depths whose origin remains unclear. Here, we propose a mechanism that could generate seismic discontinuities beneath subduction zones with depth distributions consistent with some of the observed mid-mantle reflectors. By coupling thermo-mechanical subduction models with pressure-dependent fabric calculations, we show that gradual slip transitions in bridgmanite with depth can manifest anisotropic discontinuities near 1000 km, which can deepen depending on the extent of accumulated deformation. This discontinuity is most pronounced in regions of strong slab-driven flow as revealed by its reflection coefficients, the strength of which varies with distance and azimuth. While our models predict ~ 1.5% contrast in fast versus slow shear wave velocities in terms of radial anisotropy, our full waveform simulations show that the discontinuity is detectable with array seismological methods. These results suggest that mid-mantle reflectors near subduction zones may be strain-induced, providing an additional mechanism that links mantle flow, mineral physics, and seismic observations. item.description: Divergent models persist for the emergence of animals. item.description: Deep-sea holobionts adapt to extreme environmental fluctuations, but the molecular mechanisms underlying resilience remain poorly understood. We investigated the vesicomyid clam Archivesica marissinica and its sulfur-oxidizing symbionts during sulfide shortage via in situ transplant experiments at the Haima cold seep. Transplanting clams to sulfide-depleted conditions (moderate at HM-3 and severe at HM-2) revealed distinct response patterns of host-symbiont interaction. Symbionts may mitigate sulfide loss by shifting from sulfide oxidation to thiosulfate oxidation, supported by thiosulfate generated through host sulfide detoxification pathways. Notably, symbiont abundance remained stable under moderate sulfide shortage (HM-3), accompanied by down-regulation of host endosomal maturation and fusion with lysosomes, potentially limiting symbiont turnover. Conversely, severe sulfide shortage (HM-2) was associated with up-regulation of lysosomal pathways and lower symbiont abundance. These results demonstrate tiered molecular adaptations—metabolic flexibility and shifts in symbiont dynamics—enabling holobiont resilience to spatially heterogeneous sulfide availability in deep-sea seeps, supporting ecosystem stability. item.dc:creator: Marc-Élie Adaimé

item.description: Grass (Poaceae) pollen is largely overlooked in investigations of grassland evolution because the pollen of most species cannot be differentiated using traditional optical microscopy. However, the combination of superresolution microscopy and deep learning enables the capture and quantification of distinct morphological variation across the pollen of grass species. Using a semisupervised deep-learning strategy, we trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs) on superresolution images of known modern and unlabeled fossil grass pollen. We used learned CNN features to estimate taxonomic diversity and discriminate between C 3 and C 4 grass species—applying Shannon entropy as a measure of morphological variability and a gradient-boosted decision tree as a classifier of photosynthetic type. We validated the method on modern grass pollen assemblages and then applied our trained models to fossil assemblages from a 25,000-y lake-sediment record from Mt. Kenya, correlating shifts in grass diversity through time with changes in atmospheric CO 2 concentration and proxy records of local temperature, precipitation, and fire occurrence. Our data show that the species diversity of these montane grasslands declined substantially between 21,500 and 16,000 years ago, coincident with the most severe regional cooling of the last ice age, and that the fraction of C 4 grasses gradually decreased after the late-glacial–Holocene transition, associated with higher temperatures and decreasing fire activity. Our results demonstrate that CNN features of pollen morphology can advance palynological analysis and enable robust estimation of changes in grass diversity and C 4 grass abundance in ancient grassland ecosystems. item.description: Although increasing evidence implicates subchondral bone alterations in osteoarthritis, the spatial organization of subchondral bone remodeling remains unclear. Applying spatial transcriptomics to human subchondral bone, we identify a spatially conserved osteogenic core-halo architecture that displays transcriptional reprogramming in sclerotic microenvironments. Spatial dependency and a customized cell-cell communication framework reveal disrupted osteoblast-osteoclast spatial coupling, enhanced osteoblast-mesenchymal interactions, and identify FN1-SDC2 and COL1A1-DDR2 as candidate stromal-osteogenic signaling axes that may contribute to aberrant bone remodeling. Additionally, we present the in situ transcriptional landscape of osteocytes and reveal its potential regulatory role in aberrant bone remodeling. We further delineate a continuum of spatial ecotypes exhibiting distinct enrichment, spatial topology reorganization, and inter-ecotype communication rewiring across pathological states. Metabolic flux inference additionally reveals substrate-limited, stressed states across multiple ecotypes in sclerotic microenvironments. Collectively, our findings provide critical insights into aberrant subchondral bone remodeling in osteoarthritis and offer a valuable framework for future mechanistic studies and therapeutic exploration. item.description: The early India-Eurasia collision induced widespread tectonic deformation and vigorous magmatism throughout southern Tibet, yet the dynamic connections between magmatism and crustal evolution in the collision zone remain controversial. item.description: A long-standing debate concerns whether arc magmas are generated by melting of a slab- metasomatized mantle wedge or by direct melting and dehydration of mélange diapirs. item.description: The Jiangnan Orogenic Belt in South China hosts numerous world-class Au-Sb-W deposits, with different mineralization styles, including Au-W and Au-Sb. item.description: Mercury (Hg) isotopes, particularly mass-independent fractionation (MIF; expressed as Δ199Hg), serve as a powerful tracer for tracking the recycling of surficial materials into Earth’s deep interior. Together with Sr-Nd isotope constraints indicating minor crustal contamination, these observations rule out a crustal origin for the negative Δ199Hg anomalies and instead reflect a mantle source modified by recycled terrestrial Hg. The near-zero Δ199Hg values of the Nicobar Fan sediments (−0.01 to 0.03‰) indicate that the recycled terrestrial Hg in the mantle source is unlikely to originate from the Nicobar Fan but more likely reflects locally derived Sumatran terrigenous sediments. Three-endmember mixing models coupling Δ199Hg with Sr–Nd isotopes further indicate that the subducted sediment contribution was dominated by Nicobar Fan sediments but included a smaller proportion of Sumatra terrigenous component carrying the negative Hg-MIF signature, with total sediment additions of <5 wt% beneath the Sumatra stratovolcanoes and ∼5–10 wt% beneath the Toba volcanic system. item.description: Located in the eastern Jiangnan Orogen, the Dazhou deposit is a quartz vein-type gold deposit in the E-hu gold mineralization concentration area, northeastern Jiangxi Province, South China. Hosted by tuffaceous slate and sandy slate of the Neoproterozoic Shuangqiaoshan Group, the deposit’s hydrothermal evolution, sulfur source, and gold mineralization mechanism remain poorly constrained. This study employs integrated petrographic observations, in situ trace element analyses of quartz and sulfides, and sulfur isotope analyses of sulfides to unravel the evolution of the ore-forming system and the processes governing gold enrichment. Three hydrothermal stages are identified: an early quartz-pyrite-arsenopyrite stage (Stage I), a main quartz-polysulfide stage (Stage II), and a late quartz-carbonate stage (Stage III). Trace element compositions of quartz and sulfides record systematic variations in fluid chemistry throughout mineralization. Relative to Stage I, Stage II quartz and sulfides exhibit enhanced trace element enrichment and more complex elemental associations, signaling progressive evolution of the hydrothermal fluids during the main mineralization event. Sulfides display consistently negative δ34S values (−16.63 ‰ to −8.94 ‰), which, in conjunction with geological constraints, indicate that sulfur was primarily sourced from reduced sulfur species preserved within the Shuangqiaoshan Group and subsequently remobilized by hydrothermal fluids. The transition from pyrite-arsenopyrite to pyrite-arsenopyrite-pyrrhotite- chalcopyrite assemblages, coupled with a weakening of Au-As correlations in pyrite, indicates that decreasing sulfur fugacity modified sulfide stability fields and altered gold incorporation mechanisms. The Dazhou deposit is interpreted as an orogenic gold system formed via structurally controlled hydrothermal circulation and fluid-rock interaction. The evolution of reduced sulfur availability and sulfur fugacity exerted critical controls on sulfide transformation and gold enrichment in the Jiangnan Orogen. item.description: Sulfur (S), a moderately siderophile and volatile element, may have been delivered to Earth during the planet’s main stage of accretion. Alternatively, it may have been supplied by the late veneer, after the core was fully segregated from the mantle. Mid-ocean ridge basalts present a systematic depletion in the heavier S isotope, 34S, relative to chondrites. This has been suggested to reflect isotopic fractionation during core–mantle differentiation or during evaporative loss from Earth’s magma ocean. Two studies have estimated the metal–silicate S isotope fractionation but yielded conflicting results. Laboratory experiments suggest that equilibrium fractionation favors the heavy 34S in metal during metal–silicate equilibria. However, the magnitude of the 34S/32S fractionation between metal and silicate appears too small to explain the composition of mid-ocean ridge basalts. In contrast, ab-initio calculations predict fractionation in the opposite direction, with a much smaller magnitude. Here, we present a series of experiments conducted with the triple-isotope technique. This approach allows for a robust determination of sulfur isotope fractionation between metal and silicate. We also report a set of conventional time-series experiments with variable starting isotopic compositions, and compare the results from both approaches. The reported results confirm that metal–silicate equilibration produces significant 34S-depletion in silicates, with a magnitude of 0.65 ± 0.28‰ at 1673 K, in agreement with previous experimental work. This fractionation is parametrized as a function of temperature to account for Earth’s mantle composition following 1000 ∗ ln α M e t . - S i l . ≈ a / T 2 = 1.819 ± 0.784 × 10 6 K - 2 . This fractionation can explain most depleted mantle estimates; however, additional processes such as the effect of high-pressure equilibrium, sulfide–melt equilibria, or long-term mantle recycling may contribute to the observed Earth’s mantle regional variations. item.description: Granite-related Sn–W polymetallic deposits represent a major global source of Sn and W, yet the mechanisms driving their co-enrichment with chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Ag) remain poorly understood. Along the southwestern margin of the South China Block, four equally spaced magmatic suites, ranging from Early Paleozoic to Cretaceous in age and from granitic to mafic in composition, host large to giant Sn–W polymetallic deposits with diverse metal associations, providing an ideal natural laboratory to address this issue. By integrating new and published geochronological and geochemical data, we identify four magmatic pulses during both the Early Paleozoic (442.2–402.4 Ma) and the Cretaceous (117.1–77.4 Ma). Based on ages and metal associations, the ore-related intrusions are classified into four groups: (1) Sn–W-related Cretaceous peraluminous granites; (2) Ag-related Cretaceous metaluminous to weakly peraluminous granites; (3) Sn–W–Cu-related Early Paleozoic mafic–granitic rocks; and (4) Sn–Cu-related Cretaceous mafic–granitic rocks. These granite types display distinct elemental and isotopic signatures, reflecting diverse origins and evolutionary processes: (1) Sn–W-related granites formed via mica (muscovite and biotite)-dehydration melting of Proterozoic metapelites; (2) Ag-related granites derived from amphibole-dehydration melting of Proterozoic amphibolites; (3) Sn–W–Cu-related granites originated from mica-dehydration melting of Proterozoic metapelites with additional input from asthenospheric mantle-derived mafic magmas; and (4) Sn–Cu-related granites stemmed from a similar metapelitic source but with contributions from enriched lithospheric mantle-derived mafic magmas. These petrogenetic models reveal that Sn–W-dominated mineralization is primarily linked to mica-dehydration melting of metapelites, whereas chalcophile element-dominated mineralization is associated with mantle-derived magmas or amphibole-dehydration melting of mafic lower crust derived from such magmas. These two systems, coupled via the injection of mafic magmas into metapelite-derived granitic magmas, control the co-enrichment of Sn–W and chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu) within a single deposit. These magmatic–metallogenic frameworks demonstrate the role of a three-tiered cascading model—ranging from crustal sources (metapelites vs. amphibolites), through melting mechanisms (muscovite-, biotite-, and amphibole-dehydration melting), to mantle inputs (enriched lithospheric vs. asthenospheric mantle)—in controlling the co-enrichment of Sn–W and chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu). This cascading model is governed by first-order geodynamic triggers, including polyphase tectonic evolution and unique geodynamic mechanisms. Based on these considerations, we define three diagnostic criteria—petrological, elemental, and isotopic—that can effectively distinguish Sn–W–Cu systems from Sn–W-only systems. Thus, this work greatly advances our understanding of metallogenic specialization in granitic systems, and holds significant implications for exploring diverse Sn–W polymetallic deposits in analogous settings worldwide. item.description: The West Qinling gold metallogenic province is one of China’s largest gold producers, yet the genesis and temporal framework of its gold deposits remain highly debated. Variable bell-shape REE patterns and positive correlations between EuN and Eu* in scheelite indicate an oxidizing environment, controlled by variations in fluid salinity and Na-REE coupled substitution mechanism. Early Py1 is enriched in Co and Se and displays Co/Sb–Se/As characteristics consistent with a magmatic-hydrothermal contribution. Se-in-pyrite thermometry yields formation temperatures of up to 544 ± 36 °C for the earliest stage, decreasing to approximately 323–417 °C in later Py1 and 342 ± 11 °C for Py2. The transition from Co-rich Py1 to Co-poor, Ni-enriched Py2, together with pyrrhotite-dominated assemblages and cross-cutting chalcopyrite–pyrrhotite textures, records progressive changes in fluid chemistry and conditions of sulphide stability. Variable magnetite trace-element compositions and brecciation further indicate repeated modification during continued fluid circulation. Structural relationships demonstrate that deformation enhanced permeability along the Mary Kathleen structural architecture, promoting fluid focusing, sulphide redistribution, and local concentration within retrograde alteration zones. item.description: The mechanisms of rare metal mineralization within highly evolved granite–pegmatite systems remain a topic of debate, particularly regarding the role of magmatic–hydrothermal processes in rare metal enrichment. It exhibits a progressive lithological transition from amazonite-free granite in the lower lithological zones (LLZ) to amazonite-rich granite and pegmatite veins in the middle lithological zones (MLZ) to amazonite-poor granite in the upper lithological zone (ULZ), which formed as a result of the magmatic–hydrothermal evolution of a single granitic melt. Accordingly, this pluton provides a unique opportunity to investigate the mechanisms of rare metal mineralization through quantitatively constraining the origin and physicochemical properties of fluids, and by evaluating how these fluids drive geochemical fractionation during magmatic–hydrothermal evolution. Magmatic zircon domains (Zrn-I; δ18OZrn-I = 5.88–7.39‰) have δ18O values that reflect that of the parental granitic melt. item.description: The Jiangnan Orogen is the world's largest Au-Sb-W metallogenic belt and an ideal natural laboratory for investigating polymetallic mineralization. However, the sources of tungsten-bearing ore-forming fluids and the mechanisms of tungsten mineralization remain controversial. This study focuses on the Wangu gold deposit in the central Jiangnan Orogen. Microstructural observations and cathodoluminescence (CL) imaging distinguish two main-stage scheelite generations, Sch-1a and Sch-1b, and two late-stage scheelite generations, Sch-2a and Sch-2b. Sch-2a is not interpreted as a wholly newly precipitated scheelite generation, but rather as a fractured and fluid-modified domain of earlier Sch-1a, whereas Sch-2b records limited local reprecipitation after this late-stage disturbance. Main-stage scheelite is characterized by high Sr, low Mo, variable LREE-depleted to MREE-HREE-enriched REE patterns with pronounced positive Eu anomalies, and relatively radiogenic 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.74732–0.75164), indicating precipitation from a metamorphic-hydrothermal fluid with a substantial crustal component, consistent with the characteristics of scheelite in orogenic gold systems. Sch-1a, the dominant scheelite generation, is closely associated with quartz and ankerite, and represents the principal tungsten precipitation event. Its pronounced positive Eu anomaly suggests precipitation under highly reducing conditions, whereas its stable association with ankerite indicates a neutral to weakly alkaline fluid environment. These conditions were probably favored by structurally controlled fluid ascent along NWW-trending faults. Pressure decrease during this process may have promoted local phase separation, CO₂ escape, and pH increase, thereby providing a plausible mechanism for efficient Sch-1a precipitation under reducing, neutral to weakly alkaline conditions. Although all scheelite generations show geochemical features consistent with formation under overall reducing conditions, the systematic decrease in positive Eu anomalies from Sch-1a to Sch-1b and then to late-stage scheelite indicates a progressive increase in oxygen fugacity during fluid evolution. item.description: The systematic spatial differentiation of metals within a single stratigraphic framework is a defining feature of strata-bound mineral systems, yet the physical processes that drive such zonation remain poorly constrained. Steep solubility gradients of CuCl2 − focus copper precipitation in high-temperature zones (≤ 350 °C) proximal to the heat source, while the relative stability of Au(HS)2 − facilitates gold transport to distal mixing fronts. item.description: Deep strike-slip faults regulate hydrothermal fluid circulation and hydrocarbon migration, exerting a fundamental control on hydrocarbon accumulation in carbonate reservoirs of cratonic basins. Their complex geometry, however, makes strike-slip faults difficult to characterize, limiting our understanding of how they control hydrocarbon accumulation. Hydrothermal fluids provide multi-parameter proxies for characterizing strike-slip faults. This review addresses three key gaps: (i) the unclear vertical connectivity of strike-slip faults across different strata as recorded by hydrothermal fluids; (ii) the poorly constrained map-view connectivity and segmentation of strike-slip faults reflected by hydrothermal variations; and (iii) the unresolved temporal coupling among hydrothermal activity, strike-slip fault reactivation, and hydrocarbon accumulation. Using the central Sichuan Basin as a natural laboratory, Vertically, hydrothermal activity is strongest in the Dengying Formation, followed by the Qixia–Maokou Formations, and weakest in the Longwangmiao Formation, indicating variable vertical connectivity of deep strike-slip faults across different strata. In map view, stronger hydrothermal activity and complex mineral assemblages in southern and eastern sectors suggest enhanced fault connectivity. U–Pb dating identifies three fault-reactivation stages during the Caledonian–Early Hercynian (520 Ma–400 Ma), Late Hercynian–Indosinian (320 Ma–200 Ma), and Yanshanian–Himalayan (130 Ma–20 Ma). These fault-controlled hydrothermal processes regulated fluid migration, reservoir modification, and hydrocarbon accumulation, resulting in the multi-strata stacked accumulation pattern in central Sichuan. The Spatial Temporal coupling between fault reactivation and hydrothermal pulses promoted source rock maturation, modified reservoir quality, enhanced migration pathways, triggered TSR, and altered hydrocarbon phase states. This study demonstrates that hydrothermal fluids are a novel proxy for reconstructing deep strike-slip fault connectivity, reactivation history, and hydrocarbon-controlling roles in deep carbonate reservoirs. item.description: The base of cratonic lithospheric mantle (cratonic root) is a key volatile-rich reservoir (e.g., carbon and halogens), formed through long-term metasomatism by deep-derived incipient melts, whose reactivation has been proposed to drive climatic change over the course of Earth history. Compared to mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORBs), lamproites and lamprophyres show higher F (1200−6040 ppm) and Br/Cl ratios (3.3−30.0 × 10−3), which are inconsistent with a degassing signature and instead reflect enrichment of F and Br in their mantle sources. In contrast, nephelinites have high F (1470−2430 ppm) but MORB-like Br/Cl ratios (1.3−2.4 × 10−3), consistent with Br loss during fluid exsolution. These results agree with published halogen data for carbonatites, kimberlites, inclusions in diamonds and cratonic peridotites, showing that cratonic roots worldwide are enriched in F and Br. Field study indicates that the North Altyn accretionary complex is composed of ophiolites, magmatic rocks, high-pressure/low-temperature metamorphic rocks, Neoproterozoic tectonic fragments, intraoceanic arc relics, and sedimentary sequences. Sedimentary samples collected from different units are dominated by volcanic detritus and display low compositional maturity, consistent with deposition in forearc to backarc basin settings. Detrital zircon U-Pb geochronology yields maximum depositional ages ranging from ca. 505 Ma to ca. 402 Ma and reveals an overall northward-younging trend across the accretionary complex. Variations in detrital zircon age spectra and Hf isotopic compositions indicate distinct provenance signatures and temporal changes in sediment supply. These data demonstrate that subduction of the North Altyn Ocean initiated before ca. 540 Ma and persisted with a southern-dipping polarity until at least ca. 419 Ma, as indicated by the predominance of detritus from a southern sediment source (Central Altyn Terrane). A significant provenance shift to bidirectional sediment input occurred between ca. 419 Ma and ca. 402 Ma, recording the onset of amalgamation between the North and Central Altyn terranes. Furthermore, our new provenance data reveal the presence of an Ediacaran intraoceanic arc and provide the first sedimentary evidence linking it to the South Altyn orogenesis, thereby constraining the timing of amalgamation and exhumation across the entire Altyn orogen. item.description: Although skarn polymetallic systems represent major global reservoirs of the critical metal indium (In), the enrichment mechanisms and fluid evolution in distal skarn systems remain poorly constrained. The results demonstrate that In incorporation into sphalerite is primarily facilitated by CuIn coupled substitution (Cu+ + In3+ ↔ 2Zn2+), with subordinate participation of Sn and additional regulation by Cd-related lattice strain. Ab initio simulations further demonstrate that substitution configurations involving In, Sn, Cu, Cd, and Fe exert different influences on lattice strain and formation energy, providing a crystal-chemical constraint on In incorporation. Consequently, sphalerite records a fluid cooling evolution driven by wall-rock buffering and meteoric water influx: SpIa formed at ∼500 °C under moderate to high fS₂ conditions favorable for In enrichment (up to 300 ppm); SpIb-SpII precipitated during 380 to 290 °C, with SpII attaining peak In concentrations (up to 744.97 ppm); whereas SpIII formed at <250 °C and low fS₂, where stable In incorporation was inhibited (0.4 ppm). item.description: This study presents petrographic and major- and trace-element data on olivine from eight kimberlite bodies in the Kuoyka field (Yakutia, Siberian Craton), which include pyroclastic and coherent varieties and have a wide range of geochemical and isotopic compositions, in order to investigate kimberlitic melt evolution and interaction with the lithospheric mantle. Olivine compositions define three populations: Mg-rich macrocryst cores (Mg# 0.90–0.94); Fe-rich macrocryst cores (Mg# 0.83–0.88); and Al-Ca-Ti-rich olivines (Mg# 0.87–0.92). Mg-rich cores are xenocrysts from depleted, variably metasomatised peridotite near the spinel-garnet transition. Screened cores yield 815 ± 50 °C and 3.5 ± 0.3 GPa using Al-in-olivine thermometry and iterative projection onto local geotherms. Fe-rich cores have a megacryst affinity and record protokimberlitic melt fractionation coupled with interaction with pre-existing Fe-Ti-rich mantle lithologies. Al-Ca-Ti-rich olivine records early involvement of kimberlitic or aillikite-like protokimberlitic melts. This population represents early liquidus olivine in coherent kimberlite, whereas similar domains in pyroclastic kimberlites may include melt-modified mantle olivine. Most macrocrysts with Mg-rich or Fe-rich cores are zoned, with Internal zone (IZ-2) and main rims recording magmatic growth and differentiation. Pipe-to-pipe variations in olivine populations and core-rim Mg# indicate sampling of a regionally widespread Mg-rich peridotitic component and variable contributions from Fe-Ti-rich mantle domains. The olivine results and the published mantle xenolith record indicate predominantly shallow to intermediate sampling of a strongly modified and potentially thinned craton-margin lithosphere near the graphite-diamond boundary, although local sampling of deeper, potentially diamond-stable mantle cannot be excluded. item.description: ABSTRACT The Meyon gold deposit is located within the Mogok Metamorphic Belt (MMB), approximately 150 km southeast of Yangon, in the northwestern part of Mon State, Myanmar. These results demonstrate that gold mineralization resulted from the upward migration of CO 2 ‐rich fluids along shear zones, followed by pressure decrease, phase separation, and cooling. The study provides a well‐constrained genetic model and highlights the exploration potential of the Mergui Belt for orogenic gold deposits. item.description: The bedrock of Jutulsessen, central Dronning Maud Land (East Antarctica), comprises orthogneisses and migmatites interlayered with mafic and pelitic granulites of the Mesoproterozoic Maud Belt. These rocks record high-grade metamorphism associated with the Ediacaran–Cambrian orogeny during the assembly of Gondwana. Here, we reconstruct the pressure-temperature (P–T) evolution of the granulites using mineral assemblages, inclusion suites, reaction textures, and phase equilibria (pseudosection) modelling. The granulites record a clockwise P–T path, which involves prograde burial to high-pressure granulite-facies conditions, followed by decompression at elevated temperatures and subsequent cooling and hydration at lower-grade conditions. Garnet growth is associated with amphibolite- to granulite-facies inclusion assemblages. Peak-pressure conditions are preserved in low-strain mafic lenses containing the assemblage garnet + clinopyroxene + quartz + plagioclase, and by the occurrence of kyanite + rutile in pelitic rocks. Garnet-breakdown textures in mafic rocks and the transformation of kyanite-bearing assemblages to sillimanite- and cordierite-bearing assemblages in pelitic rocks record high-temperature decompression. Microtextures in the pelitic granulites indicate that decompression was locally accompanied by partial melting, resulting in garnet breakdown and regrowth linked to melt production. Retrograde cooling is reflected by clinopyroxene exsolution and fluid-assisted amphibole growth in mafic rocks, as well as by biotite growth in supracrustal rocks. The reconstructed P–T path records crustal thickening and deep burial, followed by high-temperature decompression and exhumation, consistent with tectonic models for the Ediacaran–Cambrian assembly of Gondwana.
